idea.title: AI Accessibility Reviewer

fm.title: AI Accessibility Reviewer
fm.beneficiaries: Designers, product managers, developers, QA, accessibility specialists, and organisations building digital products for diverse users.
fm.demo_promise: An AI tool that analyses designs for risk across visual, interaction, content and cognitive domains — explaining what the issue is, who it affects, why it matters, its severity, and how the design could improve. Shown through a sample UI with AI findings and suggested fixes.

idea.body:
Problem

Accessibility is considered late in product development. Designers and developers don't know what issues exist until formal QA or an accessibility audit, making fixes costly and delaying inclusive design.

Proposed solution

Analyse designs early and explain findings rather than just flagging them. Accessibility is often reduced to visual constraints; building at scale for education and underserved users needs a broader view than standard visual guidelines.

What they said they'd demo

An AI tool that analyses designs for risk across visual, interaction, content and cognitive domains — explaining what the issue is, who it affects, why it matters, its severity, and how the design could improve. Shown through a sample UI with AI findings and suggested fixes.

fm.demo_promise: End-to-end agent taking a suspicious SMS/WhatsApp screenshot: extract via AI/OCR, identify claims and URLs, retrieve trusted policies and known scam patterns via RAG, verify URL/sender/claims against trusted sources, produce a risk assessment (Likely Safe / Needs Verification / High Risk) with an explainable evidence trail and a recommended next action. Both a legitimate and a scam message shown, to prove it does not label everything fraud.

idea.body:
Problem

People receive suspicious messages, payment requests and links daily. Existing solutions classify them as scam or not-scam, which produces false positives and never establishes whether the claims in a message are actually true.

Proposed solution

TrustLens investigates rather than classifies — RAG over trusted policies and scam patterns, plus verification tools for URLs, sender identity and claims such as transactions or bills.

What they said they'd demo

End-to-end agent taking a suspicious SMS/WhatsApp screenshot: extract via AI/OCR, identify claims and URLs, retrieve trusted policies and known scam patterns via RAG, verify URL/sender/claims against trusted sources, produce a risk assessment (Likely Safe / Needs Verification / High Risk) with an explainable evidence trail and a recommended next action. Both a legitimate and a scam message shown, to prove it does not label everything fraud.

idea.title: AI-Powered Digital Readiness & Assessment Companion

fm.title: AI-Powered Digital Readiness & Assessment Companion
fm.beneficiaries: Children who are first-time digital learners in rural and government schools; teachers and assessors who currently spend their time on basic device help; education departments, NGOs, EdTech companies and assessment organisations.
fm.demo_promise: A first-time learner taken through mouse practice, keyboard interaction, listening, microphone and voice check, navigation, AI guidance when stuck, a readiness check, then a game-like oral reading activity with background speech analysis and a simple teacher-facing result.

idea.body:
Problem

Many children in rural and government schools have little experience with computers or tablets, and struggle with mouse, keyboard, navigation, microphone and headphones before any learning activity can start. Formal assessment also makes children anxious, which changes how they read and speak.

Proposed solution

Combine device readiness, AI guidance and child-friendly assessment in one environment. The child learns the device through a game, then the same environment becomes the assessment — reading as part of a story rather than sitting a test. The child experiences a game; the teacher receives structured results.

What they said they'd demo

A first-time learner taken through mouse practice, keyboard interaction, listening, microphone and voice check, navigation, AI guidance when stuck, a readiness check, then a game-like oral reading activity with background speech analysis and a simple teacher-facing result.

Problem

The Tekdi Agent Platform hosts real, working intelligence that teams already rely on, but it is locked inside one custom harness and cannot be used from Claude, Antigravity or wherever people actually work. That caps internal adoption and caps turning the intelligence into something licensable.

idea.title: Give the Brain a Memory for How We Actually Deliver

fm.title: Give the Brain a Memory for How We Actually Deliver
fm.beneficiaries: Delivery and engineering teams reusing past decisions, PMs and architects scoping new engagements, new joiners ramping onto a project, and anyone drafting proposals or case studies who needs real delivery history.
fm.demo_promise: Feed the skill a real conversation about a delivery decision and show it land — correctly shaped, correctly routed, correctly attributed — in the right brain repo, without a human picking where it goes.

idea.body:
Problem

The company brain knows who the clients are, what was sold and who was involved — but almost nothing about how the work is actually built. There is no structured place for why Postgres was chosen over Mongo, why an integration was reworked mid-flight, what a retro flagged, or what a senior engineer would tell a team walking into a similar build. That knowledge lives in Slack threads and people's heads and evaporates when someone rolls off.

Proposed solution

Design a delivery/engineering knowledge schema — decisions, trade-offs, retro learnings — with the same discipline the wiki already uses (typed frontmatter, sourced provenance, additive schema versioning), and extend the ingest skill to recognise this content and route it to the right repo.

What they said they'd demo

Feed the skill a real conversation about a delivery decision and show it land — correctly shaped, correctly routed, correctly attributed — in the right brain repo, without a human picking where it goes.

Notes

This wiki is a live pilot of that schema. Its decisions/ and learnings/ entities are the proposal, running against real work.

idea.title: Trace to Trust

fm.title: Trace to Trust
fm.beneficiaries: Quality-conscious buyers and exporters.
fm.demo_promise: A working demo of a full journey end to end — capture at origin through to the trust-check at the end.

idea.body:
Problem

Trust in a food label rests almost entirely on the honesty of everyone in the chain and the paperwork they choose to keep. The challenge is to let food carry its own verifiable history from origin to the person eating it.

Proposed solution

Capture real-world moments as they happen — a boat leaving harbour, a catch iced, a plot sown, a warehouse hop — and let someone far down the chain reconstruct the story and have reason to believe it. Four questions a strong solution must answer: trust without a trusted middleman (tamper-evidence and provenance); capture by real people with limited digital literacy and patchy connectivity; what the end user actually sees when they scan; and whether the approach survives a completely different food chain without a rebuild.

What they said they'd demo

A working demo of a full journey end to end — capture at origin through to the trust-check at the end.

Notes

Fisheries (EU catch certificates) and agriculture (farm plot to retail pack) given as illustrations, not requirements.

idea.title: What's Actually In This Pack?

fm.title: What's Actually In This Pack?
fm.beneficiaries: Anyone buying packaged food.
fm.demo_promise: Track A: extraction and aggregation, with documents and a spreadsheet of results. Track B: a working prototype. Teams may attempt either or both; each track is judged on its own merits — breadth is not rewarded, depth is.

idea.body:
Problem

Every packaged food sold in India carries a legally complete label, but interpreting it is left to the shopper — impossible for someone with lower literacy or no intent to read labels. It is a translation-and-presentation problem, which is to say a UX problem. Assume a low-end Android phone, patchy connectivity, a noisy shop aisle, three seconds of attention and one free hand.

Proposed solution

Handle at least two of the things labels hide: sugar as an abstraction (normalise independently of a manufacturer-chosen serving size, keep added sugar distinct from intrinsic); ingredient splitting (re-aggregate sugars, refined flours, fats and salts into families and re-sort — the hardest and most valuable part); category truth (an ice cream that is legally a frozen dessert); claim contradiction; opaque and animal-derived additives; sodium; and unrealistic serving sizes.

What they said they'd demo

Track A: extraction and aggregation, with documents and a spreadsheet of results. Track B: a working prototype. Teams may attempt either or both; each track is judged on its own merits — breadth is not rewarded, depth is.

Notes

Explicit anti-patterns in the submission: barcode lookup into an existing database; a red/amber/green dial nobody reads correctly; three paragraphs of LLM nutrition advice; a demo that works only on the two tested packs; an output that cannot expand "6 tsp total sugars" back into the six listed ingredients; and moral scoring or shaming. Track B requires testing on people outside the team, recording whether the choice switched, how long it took, the reason in their own words, and at least one case where the output misled someone.

idea.title: Who's Allowed to Write to the Brain?

idea.body:
Problem

Anyone using the ingest skill today can write directly to the company brain. There is no notion of who is trusted to commit straight to the wiki versus who should propose a change for review. Fine at today's scale; uncomfortable once the brain holds delivery knowledge or client-sensitive detail.

Proposed solution

A lightweight permission model mapped from GitHub/org identity deciding direct-write versus propose-and-wait, with a review queue (a PR underneath) and a minimal web view where an approver reads the diff in plain terms and approves or rejects.

idea.title: WorkQueue - AI Work Intelligence

fm.title: WorkQueue - AI Work Intelligence
fm.beneficiaries: Employees across Tekdi working with multiple systems — developers, QA, product and project managers, designers, HR, sales, support, operations and leadership.
fm.demo_promise: A working end-to-end prototype using a small set of real integrations and a common AI work model.

idea.body:
Problem

Employees work across Gmail, Calendar/Meet, Time Tracker, GitHub/GitLab, Keka and other systems, each holding only part of their work. Discovering pending requests, follow-ups, approvals and reviews means constant application switching; tasks get missed and the same information is later reconstructed by hand for status updates and timesheets.

Proposed solution

An AI work-intelligence layer that turns scattered signals into one personalised view answering four questions: what needs my attention, why does it matter, where did it come from, what should I do next. Related activity across platforms is linked into a single Work Item with links back to the source systems, and the same evidence drafts the daily status, timesheet entry and KRA summary for review.

What they said they'd demo

A working end-to-end prototype using a small set of real integrations and a common AI work model.

decision.title: Export the complete, secret-scrubbed project as a ZIP for manual push to a private GitHub repo, instead of an automated backup.

fm.decision: Export the complete, secret-scrubbed project as a ZIP for manual push to a private GitHub repo, instead of an automated backup.

options_considered.option: Create a new private repo and push directly via the connected GitHub App/connector
options_considered.why_not: The GitHub App installation isn't authorized to create repositories, and the connector wasn't installed with repo access for this project in this sandbox — so it authenticates but cannot create or push to a repo.

fm.chosen_because: It was the only path available to get the work off the sandbox and into the user's hands without direct GitHub write access.
fm.tradeoff_accepted: Backup requires a manual step from the user (downloading and pushing the ZIP) rather than a fully automated push, and the sandbox's local commit history isn't carried over unless the user re-initializes git before pushing.
fm.revisit_if: Once the GitHub App installation is granted repository-creation/write access for this project (or another form of repo write access is arranged).

decision.body:
Context

Needed to get a verified, secret-scrubbed backup of the full Joomla2Node project out of the sandbox and into a private GitHub repo, but had no direct git/GitHub write access from the sandbox environment.

Options

Direct push via the GitHub App/connector was the natural first choice but was blocked by permissions — see options_considered.

Rationale

Exporting a ZIP was the only remaining path that didn't require GitHub write access, and the export was verified clean on a secret scan before handoff.

Consequences

The user has to manually push the ZIP to a private repo themselves; the automated, versioned backup path is deferred until the GitHub App's installation/permissions are fixed for this project.

learning.title: A full repo-wide secret scan ahead of an external backup caught a real-looking hardcoded Google API key vendored inside the BaForms third-party PHP source.

fm.learning: A full repo-wide secret scan ahead of an external backup caught a real-looking hardcoded Google API key vendored inside the BaForms third-party PHP source.
fm.evidence: The key was found and redacted from the vendored PHP source, and a repo-wide secret scan run afterward came back clean.
fm.generalises_to: Run a full secret scan before any external backup, export, or publish step — including on vendored third-party code the team didn't write itself, since bundled dependencies can carry live-looking credentials nobody on the team put there.
fm.cost_of_lesson: Under an hour — one dedicated repo-wide scan-and-redact pass before export.

learning.body:
What happened

While preparing the project for an external GitHub backup, a full security cleanup pass turned up a real-looking hardcoded Google API key vendored inside the BaForms third-party PHP source (not code the team wrote).

Evidence

The key was redacted from the vendored source, and a repo-wide secret scan run afterward returned clean.

What we'd do differently

Not stated this round.
